import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components'

From v0.21, Seamless Auth can act as an OpenID Provider. Any app that speaks OpenID Connect or
OAuth 2.0 (Grafana, GitLab, Argo CD, Auth.js, Spring Security, a reverse proxy, your own backend)
signs users in through hosted Seamless pages with passkeys and the other methods your instance
allows, and gets standard ID tokens and access tokens back. The app needs no Seamless SDK.

Use this guide when an app should sign users in with standard OIDC instead of a Seamless adapter,
when a backend or job needs tokens for an API (client credentials), or when your own API should
accept tokens the provider issued. For apps you build yourself on a supported framework, the
[server adapters](/build/server-sdks) are still the shorter path. For native, desktop and CLI apps,
read this page first and then [Sign-In For Native, Desktop And CLI Apps](/build/native-apps-oidc).

<Aside type="note" title="Status">
  The OpenID Provider ships in v0.21. It needs `seamless-auth-api` from v0.21 and the new
  `seamless-auth-oidc-provider` service (npm `@seamless-auth/oidc-provider`, image
  `ghcr.io/fells-code/seamless-auth-oidc-provider`). Sign-out (RP-initiated logout) and the device
  authorization grant are still being built. Their sections below are placeholders.
</Aside>

---

## Architecture

The provider is a separate public service, the **login edge**, in front of the private API. The API
stays bearer-only and cookie-free, and keeps every key and every piece of provider state.

```text
any OIDC app ──► seamless-auth-oidc-provider   (public: OIDC endpoints, hosted pages, cookies)
                      │  its own service token (SEAMLESS_OIDC_SERVICE_TOKEN)
                      ▼
               seamless-auth-api                (private, no cookies) ── Postgres
```

- **The edge** is built on [`oidc-provider`](https://github.com/panva/node-oidc-provider) 9.x. It
  serves discovery, `/authorize`, `/token`, `/userinfo`, `/jwks`, introspection, revocation and the
  hosted sign-in and consent pages. It holds no private keys and no database.
- **The API** stores the provider's grants, codes and tokens in its own `oidc_payloads` table,
  reached through `/oidc/*` routes that accept only the edge's service token. It signs every token
  with the provider key set (`OIDC_JWKS_*`) after checking that the user has a live session, that
  the claims match what the session earned, and that the client may use the audience and scopes.
- **Sign-in is first-party.** The hosted pages sign users in through the edge's own adapter routes
  (`/auth/*`), the same way any Seamless app does. A provider sign-in is an ordinary session in the
  API's `sessions` table, with every first-party protection applied, and ending that session ends
  provider access at once.
- **Provider tokens are not first-party tokens.** They carry `iss` equal to `oidc_issuer` (never the
  API's `ISSUER`) and are signed with a separate key set, so the first-party verifiers in the
  Seamless adapters reject them, and the verify-only guards reject first-party tokens.

The design is recorded in
[ADR 0001](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-api/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-openid-provider.md).

---

## Deploy The Edge

### 1. Pick the issuer hostname

The issuer is the edge's public URL, for example `https://login.example.com`. The API refuses an
issuer that breaks any of these rules:

- It uses `https` (plain `http` is allowed only on a loopback host outside production).
- It has no query or fragment.
- It differs from the API's own `ISSUER`.
- Its host is `rpid` or a subdomain of it, because passkeys on the hosted pages are bound to
  `rpid`.

Pick the hostname to fit the `rpid` you have. Changing `rpid` orphans every passkey already
registered.

### 2. Turn the provider on in the API

Set these on the API (see [Environment Variables](/reference/environment-variables) for the rest):

| Variable                           | Required     | What                                                                                                                         |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `OIDC_PROVIDER_ENABLED`            | yes          | Seeds `oidc_provider_enabled`. While off, every `/oidc/*` route answers 404 and the edge refuses to start.                   |
| `OIDC_ISSUER`                      | yes          | Seeds `oidc_issuer`, the edge's public URL.                                                                                  |
| `SEAMLESS_OIDC_SERVICE_TOKEN`      | yes          | The edge's own service token secret. It must differ from `SEAMLESS_SERVICE_TOKEN`, or the API refuses to start.             |
| `OIDC_JWKS_ACTIVE_KID`             | yes          | The `kid` of the provider key that signs.                                                                                    |
| `OIDC_JWKS_KEYS`                   | yes          | A JSON JWK set of private RS256 keys, each with a unique `kid`. It must not reuse a `SEAMLESS_JWKS_*` key.                   |
| `OIDC_ALLOW_CLIENT_SECRETS`        | no           | Seeds `allow_client_secrets`. Lets an admin opt individual applications in to shared secrets. Off by default.                |
| `OIDC_THIRD_PARTY_CLIENTS_ENABLED` | no           | Seeds `third_party_clients_enabled`. Third-party applications need it, and always see a consent page.                        |
| `OIDC_HOSTED_UI`                   | no           | Seeds `hosted_ui`, the hosted page branding, as JSON. See [Brand the hosted pages](#brand-the-hosted-pages).               |

These env vars only seed `system_config` rows that do not exist yet. After the first boot, change
`oidc_provider_enabled`, `oidc_issuer`, `allow_client_secrets`, `third_party_clients_enabled` and
`hosted_ui` through the admin config routes, the dashboard or the CLI. With
`oidc_provider_enabled` on, the API refuses to start unless the issuer rules pass and the service
token and key set are present.

Also add the issuer origin (`https://login.example.com`) to the API's `origins` config. WebAuthn
ceremonies on the hosted pages are checked against that list.

<Aside type="caution" title="Two service tokens">
  `SEAMLESS_OIDC_SERVICE_TOKEN` belongs to the edge alone. `/oidc/*` accepts only that token, and
  external delivery refuses it, so a compromised edge cannot receive anyone's codes or magic links.
  Never give the edge the adapters' `SEAMLESS_SERVICE_TOKEN`.
</Aside>

### 3. Run the edge

```bash
docker run -p 5314:5314 --env-file edge.env ghcr.io/fells-code/seamless-auth-oidc-provider:latest
```

| Variable                      | Required | What                                                                                                         |
| ----------------------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `SEAMLESS_API_URL`            | yes      | The private API, as the edge reaches it.                                                                     |
| `SEAMLESS_API_ISSUER`         | no       | The API's `ISSUER`, when it differs from `SEAMLESS_API_URL`.                                                 |
| `SEAMLESS_OIDC_SERVICE_TOKEN` | yes      | The same value as on the API. At least 32 characters.                                                        |
| `SEAMLESS_JWKS_KID`           | no       | The `kid` on the service tokens the edge signs.                                                              |
| `SEAMLESS_COOKIE_SECRET`      | yes      | Signs the first-party session cookies the hosted pages use. At least 32 characters.                          |
| `OIDC_COOKIE_KEYS`            | yes      | Comma-separated provider cookie keys, each at least 32 characters. The first signs, the rest still verify. |
| `TRUST_PROXY`                 | no       | `true` when TLS ends at a proxy in front of the edge.                                                        |
| `PORT`                        | no       | Defaults to `5314`.                                                                                          |

The issuer is not an edge setting. The edge reads it from the API at startup, along with the
provider key set and `allow_client_secrets`, and refuses to start when the provider is off or the
API speaks a different version of the `/oidc/*` contract. The image has a health check on
`GET /healthz`.

To embed the edge in an existing Express app instead of running the image, mount the router at the
root of the app that serves the issuer's origin:

```ts
import express from 'express'
import { createOidcEdge } from '@seamless-auth/oidc-provider'

const edge = await createOidcEdge({
  apiUrl: process.env.SEAMLESS_API_URL!,
  serviceSecret: process.env.SEAMLESS_OIDC_SERVICE_TOKEN!,
  cookieKeys: process.env.OIDC_COOKIE_KEYS!.split(','),
  adapterCookieSecret: process.env.SEAMLESS_COOKIE_SECRET!,
  trustProxy: true,
})

const app = express()
app.set('trust proxy', 1)
app.use(edge.router)
app.listen(5314)
```

### 4. Serve it over HTTPS

Every cookie the edge sets is a `__Host-` cookie (host-only, `Secure`, `Path=/`), and the library
refuses to set a `Secure` cookie on a plain HTTP request, so the edge needs TLS in development too.
The edge itself listens on plain HTTP: terminate TLS at a proxy or load balancer and set
`TRUST_PROXY=true` so the forwarded scheme and host are trusted.

The edge answers only requests for the issuer's own scheme and host. Anything else gets
`421 {"error":"misdirected_request"}`, so a proxy that rewrites the `Host` header, or a missing
`TRUST_PROXY` behind TLS termination, shows up as a 421.

### 5. Rotate provider keys

The edge reads the provider key set from the API when it starts, so restart it after each step:

1. **Add** the new private JWK to `OIDC_JWKS_KEYS` and deploy the API. The key is published at the
   edge's `/jwks` and the old key still signs. Wait until relying parties have refreshed their
   cached JWKS.
2. **Flip** `OIDC_JWKS_ACTIVE_KID` to the new key and deploy.
3. **Retire** the old key once the longest provider token lifetime has passed.

### Endpoints

| Path                                | What                                                    |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/.well-known/openid-configuration` | Discovery                                               |
| `/authorize`                        | Authorization endpoint (code flow with PKCE only)       |
| `/token`                            | Token endpoint                                          |
| `/userinfo`                         | UserInfo                                                |
| `/jwks`                             | The provider's public keys, read from the API           |
| `/token/introspection`              | Token introspection (RFC 7662)                          |
| `/token/revocation`                 | Token revocation (RFC 7009)                             |
| `/auth/*`, `/interaction/*`         | Used by the hosted pages only, not by relying parties   |

Point every relying party at the discovery document and let it read the rest.

## Register Applications And APIs

Applications (OIDC clients) and resources (your APIs) live in the API's registry. They are managed
under `/admin/applications` and `/admin/resources`: reads need `admin:read`, and every write needs
`admin:write` plus a fresh step-up and is recorded as an `admin_oidc_*` auth event. The routes work
whether or not the provider is on, so you can register applications before the edge is deployed.

### Applications

An application has a client type and a set of grants:

| Setting                   | Values                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Client type               | `confidential` (a server that can keep a key) or `public` (SPA, native, CLI). Fixed at creation.                                                   |
| Client authentication     | `private_key_jwt` by default for confidential clients, `none` for public ones. See [Client authentication](#client-authentication).               |
| Grants                    | `authorization_code`, `refresh_token`, `client_credentials`. The default is `authorization_code` and `refresh_token`.                               |
| Redirect URIs             | Exact `https` URIs, loopback `http` on `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`, or a private-use scheme such as `com.example.app:/callback`. Up to 50.               |
| First-party               | A first-party application skips the consent page. Third-party applications need `third_party_clients_enabled`.                                    |
| Account notices           | Lets the application email or text its own users through Seamless. See [Account notices](#account-notices-from-an-application).                   |
| Disabled                  | A disabled application cannot sign anyone in or get tokens, and keeps its settings.                                                               |

The `client_id` is generated when the application is created. The registry refuses settings that
would weaken the provider, on create and on the merged result of every update:

- Public clients authenticate with PKCE alone: no secret, no keys, no `client_credentials`.
- `client_secret_jwt` cannot be chosen.
- `localhost`, fragments and embedded credentials are refused as redirect hosts, and plain `http`
  is allowed only on `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]`.
- `refresh_token` needs `authorization_code`, and `authorization_code` needs a redirect URI.

PKCE with `S256`, the code flow as the only response type, and refresh token rotation are fixed in
the edge's configuration and cannot be changed per application.

### Resources

A resource is an API your applications request access tokens for (RFC 8707). Its **identifier** is
an absolute `https`, `http` or `urn` URI, such as `https://api.example.com`. It becomes the `aud` of
every token for that API and cannot change after creation. It cannot be the API's `ISSUER` or
`oidc_issuer`, and it is never fetched.

A resource declares its scopes (for example `orders:read orders:write`) and optionally an access
token lifetime between 60 and 86,400 seconds (600 by default). Each application is then linked to
the resources it may use, with a subset of each resource's scopes. The OIDC scopes (`openid`,
`profile`, `email`, `phone`, `address`, `offline_access`) and `seamless` belong to the provider and
cannot be declared by a resource. Removing a scope from a resource removes it from every
application.

### From the admin dashboard

The [admin dashboard](/build/admin-dashboard) has an **Applications** page and a **Resources** page.

- **Applications** lists every application. Creating or editing one opens a form with the settings
  above, with each redirect URI checked as you type. Selecting an application shows its details,
  its credentials (register keys, or rotate a shared secret) and the resources and scopes it may
  use.
- **Resources** creates, edits and deletes resources and their scopes.

A shared secret is shown once, when the application is created or the secret is rotated. Only an
HMAC of it is stored, so a lost secret is rotated, never recovered.

### From the CLI

`seamless clients` manages applications and `seamless resources` manages resources. Both need an
admin role, and their writes prompt for a step-up code when the instance asks for one. (`seamless
apps` is a different command, for managed applications in the portal.)

```bash
# A confidential server-side app, authenticating with private_key_jwt
seamless clients create Docs --redirect-uri https://docs.example.com/callback \
  --jwks-uri https://docs.example.com/jwks.json

# A public desktop app
seamless clients create Desk --public \
  --redirect-uri http://127.0.0.1/callback --redirect-uri com.example.desk:/callback

seamless clients list
seamless clients get <id>
seamless clients update <id> --grants authorization_code,refresh_token --first-party
seamless clients keys <id> --jwks-file jwks.json
seamless clients rotate-secret <id>      # confirms, prints the secret once
seamless clients delete <id>             # confirms first

# An API and its scopes, then link an application to it
seamless resources create https://api.example.com --name "Orders API" \
  --scopes orders:read,orders:write --access-token-ttl 300
seamless resources list
seamless resources update <id> --scopes orders:read
seamless clients resources <id> --set https://api.example.com=orders:read
```

`create` and `update` also take `--name`, `--auth-method`, `--post-logout-uri`,
`--first-party`/`--third-party`, `--notices`/`--no-notices`, and the token lifetime flags.
`update` also takes `--disable`/`--enable`. Most commands take `--json`.

### From the API

The same operations are plain admin routes on the API, for automation:

| Route                                   | What                                                               |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `GET`/`POST /admin/applications`        | List or create applications                                        |
| `GET`/`PATCH`/`DELETE /admin/applications/:id` | Read, change or delete one (deleting also drops its grants and tokens) |
| `POST /admin/applications/:id/secret`   | Issue or rotate a shared secret                                    |
| `PUT /admin/applications/:id/keys`      | Register the JWKS or JWKS URI of a `private_key_jwt` client        |
| `GET`/`PUT /admin/applications/:id/resources` | Read or replace the resources and scopes an application may use |
| `GET`/`POST /admin/resources`           | List or create resources                                           |
| `GET`/`PATCH`/`DELETE /admin/resources/:id` | Read, change or delete one                                     |

## Client Authentication

| Client                                    | Authentication at `/token`                    |
| ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Confidential (server-side apps, services) | `private_key_jwt`, each assertion used once   |
| Public (SPA, native, CLI)                 | `none`, with PKCE                             |
| Confidential, opted in to a shared secret | `client_secret_basic` or `client_secret_post` |

**`private_key_jwt` is the default.** Register the client's public keys as a JWKS or a JWKS URI
(https), and have the client sign an assertion with the private key at the token, introspection and
revocation endpoints. RS256, PS256, ES256 and EdDSA keys are accepted. A replayed assertion is
refused as `invalid_client`. With [`openid-client`](https://github.com/panva/openid-client):

```ts
import * as oidc from 'openid-client'

const config = await oidc.discovery(
  new URL('https://login.example.com'),
  'CLIENT_ID',
  undefined,
  oidc.PrivateKeyJwt({ key: privateKey, kid: 'docs-2026' }),
)
```

**Shared secrets are an exception for apps that support nothing else.** They need two switches:
`allow_client_secrets` on the instance, which the edge reads when it starts (restart the edge after
changing it), and the shared-secret method on that application. The edge never holds a client's
secret: it asks the API to check the presented one. `client_secret_jwt` and the HS\* algorithms are
never offered.

---

## Sign Users In: Code Flow With PKCE

The authorization code flow with PKCE (`S256`) is the only flow, for every client, confidential or
public. The implicit and hybrid flows, plain PKCE and the password grant are refused.

```ts
const verifier = oidc.randomPKCECodeVerifier()
const url = oidc.buildAuthorizationUrl(config, {
  redirect_uri: 'https://docs.example.com/callback',
  scope: 'openid email',
  code_challenge: await oidc.calculatePKCECodeChallenge(verifier),
  code_challenge_method: 'S256',
  state: oidc.randomState(),
})
// Redirect the browser to `url`. On the callback:
const tokens = await oidc.authorizationCodeGrant(config, currentUrl, {
  pkceCodeVerifier: verifier,
  expectedState: state,
})
```

The user lands on the hosted sign-in page and signs in with any method enabled in `login_methods`.
A user already signed in to the edge goes straight back to the app. First-party applications have
consent implied. Third-party applications show a consent page with the application's name, the host
it returns to and the requested scopes on every authorization.

### Scopes and claims

| Scope            | Claims                                                 |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `openid`         | `sub`, `acr`, `amr`, `auth_time`                       |
| `email`          | `email`, `email_verified`                              |
| `phone`          | `phone_number`, `phone_number_verified`                |
| `seamless`       | `roles`, `org_id` (the user's default organization)    |
| `offline_access` | A refresh token. See [Refresh tokens](#refresh-tokens) |

`sub` is the user's Seamless user ID. Every ID token carries the `acr`, `amr` and `auth_time` the
API recorded for the session, whether or not the app asked for them. The claims are also in the ID
token itself, not only at `/userinfo`, because many apps read the profile from the ID token.

| Token                    | Lifetime                                                                 |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Authorization code       | 60 seconds, single use                                                   |
| ID token                 | 600 seconds                                                              |
| Access token             | 600 seconds, or the resource's own lifetime                              |
| Grant and edge session   | At most 14 days, and never longer than the user's first-party session    |

Without a `resource`, the access token is an opaque token for `/userinfo`. To call your own API,
ask for a token for it (see [Access tokens for your API](#access-tokens-for-your-api)).

### Authentication levels: `acr` and `amr`

| `acr`  | Earned by                                                                 |
| ------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `phr`  | A passkey sign-in with user verification                                  |
| `phrh` | A device-bound passkey with user verification (not a synced passkey)      |
| absent | Any sign-in without a user-verified passkey, such as an email code alone |

`phrh` satisfies a request for `phr`. `amr` lists the methods used, from `hwk` (device-bound
passkey), `swk` (synced passkey), `user` (user verification), `otp`, `sms` and `mfa` (two
different methods in one session, or a user-verified passkey).

---

## Step-Up: `acr_values`, `max_age` And `prompt=login`

Discovery lists `acr_values_supported: ["phr", "phrh"]`. An app asks for a stronger or fresher
sign-in on the authorization request:

| Parameter          | Met when                                                                                     |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `acr_values=phr`   | The session's `acr` is `phr` or `phrh`. Several values mean the weakest one listed is enough. |
| `acr_values=phrh`  | The session's `acr` is `phrh`                                                                |
| `max_age=300`      | The session's `auth_time` is at most 300 seconds old, or the user authenticated just now     |
| `prompt=login`     | The user authenticated during this authorization request                                     |

The edge decides from the session's auth context as the API reports it on every authorization, so a
step-up done in another app counts. The claims request parameter is not enabled, so `acr_values` is
the only way to ask for an `acr`.

When a requirement is not met, the hosted page asks the user to confirm on the same session: with a
passkey, or with an authenticator app code when only freshness is missing on a session that has no
`acr` (an app code never earns an `acr`). The new `acr`, `amr` and `auth_time` go into the tokens
unchanged. If the step-up still falls short, for example a synced passkey when `phrh` was asked
for, the app gets the error `unmet_authentication_requirements` instead of a token with a lower
`acr`.

```ts
const url = oidc.buildAuthorizationUrl(config, {
  redirect_uri: 'https://docs.example.com/callback',
  scope: 'openid',
  acr_values: 'phr',
  max_age: '300',
  code_challenge,
  code_challenge_method: 'S256',
})
```

The `acr`, `amr` and `auth_time` an app can rely on are the ones in the ID token. Access tokens for
an API do not carry them yet (see [Verify tokens in your API](#verify-tokens-in-your-api)).

---

## Access Tokens For Your API

An app that calls an API of its own asks for a token for it with `resource` (RFC 8707), using the
identifier of a resource the application is linked to:

```ts
const url = oidc.buildAuthorizationUrl(config, {
  redirect_uri: 'https://docs.example.com/callback',
  scope: 'openid orders:read',
  resource: 'https://api.example.com',
  code_challenge,
  code_challenge_method: 'S256',
})
```

The access token is then an RFC 9068 JWT (header `typ: at+jwt`, RS256) with:

- `aud` equal to the resource identifier, exactly as registered.
- `scope` cut to the scopes the application is allowed on that resource.
- `client_id`, `sub`, `iss`, `iat`, `exp` and `jti`.
- The resource's own lifetime.

The API checks the same links again before it signs, so a token for one resource can never carry
another resource's audience or scopes.

- A resource the application is not linked to is refused with `invalid_target`.
- An app that named one resource at authorization gets its token without repeating `resource` at
  the token endpoint, which many RP libraries never do.
- A token for a resource is not accepted at `/userinfo`.
- First-party applications get the resource scopes with the sign-in. Third-party applications list
  them on the consent page.

---

## Refresh Tokens

An application registered for the `refresh_token` grant gets a refresh token when it asks for
`offline_access`. The library honours `offline_access` only on a request with `prompt=consent`
(OpenID Connect Core section 11), so send both:

```ts
const url = oidc.buildAuthorizationUrl(config, {
  redirect_uri: 'https://docs.example.com/callback',
  scope: 'openid offline_access',
  prompt: 'consent',
  code_challenge,
  code_challenge_method: 'S256',
})
// Later:
const refreshed = await oidc.refreshTokenGrant(config, tokens.refresh_token!)
```

- **Rotation is always on.** Every refresh returns a new refresh token and the old one stops
  working.
- **Reuse ends the session.** A used refresh token presented again revokes the grant and every token
  under it, and the API ends the first-party session it was issued under, so every app on that
  session has to sign in again.
- **Refreshed ID tokens are current.** They carry the session's current `acr`, `amr` and
  `auth_time`, so a step-up since the sign-in shows up on the next refresh.
- **The session bounds it.** A refresh token works only while the user's first-party session is
  live, so ending that session in Seamless ends it.

---

## Client Credentials

A confidential application registered for `client_credentials` can get tokens for itself, with no
user, for a backend job or a service-to-service call. The token is always for a resource: the one
named with `resource`, or the application's only linked resource. An application linked to several
resources must name one.

```ts
const machine = await oidc.discovery(
  new URL('https://login.example.com'),
  'MACHINE_CLIENT_ID',
  undefined,
  oidc.PrivateKeyJwt({ key: privateKey, kid: 'jobs-2026' }),
)
const { access_token } = await oidc.clientCredentialsGrant(machine, {
  resource: 'https://api.example.com',
  scope: 'orders:read',
})
```

The token is an RFC 9068 JWT whose `sub` and `client_id` are both the application. It has no user
claims, so it can pass a scope check but never a role or step-up check. Public clients cannot use
this grant.

---

## Introspection And Revocation

`/token/introspection` (RFC 7662) and `/token/revocation` (RFC 7009) are listed in discovery and take
the same client authentication as `/token`. Both are limited to 1,200 requests a minute per client
IP, per edge instance.

**Introspection.** An application may introspect its own tokens. A resource server registers as a
confidential application linked to its resource, and may then introspect tokens whose `aud` is that
resource. Any other caller gets `{ "active": false }`. Every answer is read from the API's store, so
a token whose first-party session has ended is inactive at once.

```ts
const rs = await oidc.discovery(
  new URL('https://login.example.com'),
  'ORDERS_API_CLIENT_ID',
  undefined,
  oidc.PrivateKeyJwt({ key: rsPrivateKey, kid: 'orders-api-2026' }),
)
const status = await oidc.tokenIntrospection(rs, accessToken)
if (!status.active) throw new Error('token is no longer valid')
```

JWT access tokens can be introspected and revoked too: the edge records each one under its `jti`
when it is issued. A resource server that verifies JWTs locally still accepts a revoked token until
it expires. One that introspects sees the revocation immediately. Keep resource token lifetimes
short when that gap matters.

**Revocation.** An application revokes its own refresh or access token:

```ts
await oidc.tokenRevocation(config, tokens.refresh_token!)
```

<Aside type="caution" title="Revocation ends the app's grant, not the user's session">
  Revoking a refresh token ends that application's grant and every token under it. It does not end
  the user's first-party session, so the user's other apps stay signed in, and the next sign-in to
  this app can be silent. To sign the user out of Seamless itself, use sign-out (below). Each
  revocation is recorded in the audit log as `token_revoked`.
</Aside>

## Brand The Hosted Pages

The sign-in, step-up and consent pages are served by the edge, built on `@seamless-auth/react`.
Their branding comes from the API's `hosted_ui` config, read each time a page is served (the edge
caches the config for up to 30 seconds), so a change needs no build and no restart.

| Field        | Rules                                                                                                     |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `appName`    | 1 to 100 characters. Defaults to the instance's `app_name`.                                               |
| `logoUrl`    | An `https` URL where the image is already hosted, on a plain hostname. The instance does not store uploads. |
| `colors`     | `primary`, `onPrimary`, `background`, `surface`, `text`, `muted`, each `#rgb`, `#rrggbb` or `#rrggbbaa`.  |
| `fontFamily` | A comma-separated list of installed font names. Web fonts cannot load under the pages' CSP.               |

Setting any color turns off the pages' dark palette. The API does not check contrast, so check your
colors against WCAG AA yourself (the dashboard warns when a pair falls short).

- **Dashboard:** the **System** page, section **Hosted Page Branding**, with a preview. Saves and resets
  apply immediately.
- **CLI:**

  ```bash
  seamless config hosted-ui get
  seamless config hosted-ui set --app-name Acme --logo https://cdn.example.com/acme.svg
  seamless config hosted-ui set --primary '#0b5fff' --on-primary '#fff'
  seamless config hosted-ui reset colors.primary logoUrl
  ```

- **API:** `PATCH /system-config/admin` with `{ "hosted_ui": { ... } }` (the whole object is
  replaced, not merged) or `{ "hosted_ui": null }`. It needs `admin:write` and a fresh step-up.
- **Env:** `OIDC_HOSTED_UI` seeds it on first boot.

The pages send a strict CSP (`script-src 'self'`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`), `no-store`, `nosniff`
and `no-referrer`. The logo's origin is added to `img-src`.

## Account Notices From An Application

An application can tell one of its users something (an export is ready, a payment failed) on the
user's verified email or phone, without ever holding the address. The API sends the text inside a
fixed template that names the application and the instance, so a notice cannot pose as a Seamless
security message.

1. Turn on **account notices** for the application (`--notices` in the CLI, or the checkbox in the
   dashboard) and register it for `client_credentials`.
2. Get a client credentials token for the built-in resource `<oidc_issuer>/seamless` with scope
   `notices:send`. The API lists that resource for every application with notices on, so you do not
   create it.
3. Call `POST /applications/account-notices` **on the API** with that token as a bearer token.

```ts
const { access_token } = await oidc.clientCredentialsGrant(machine, {
  resource: 'https://login.example.com/seamless',
  scope: 'notices:send',
})

await fetch('https://auth-api.internal.example.com/applications/account-notices', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${access_token}`, 'content-type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    userId: '6f1c...', // the user's `sub`
    subject: 'Your export is ready',
    text: 'The export you asked for is ready to download.',
    actionUrl: 'https://docs.example.com/exports/42',
  }),
})
```

| Field       | Rules                                                                                          |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `userId`    | The user's `sub`. The user must hold a grant with this application.                            |
| `subject`   | One line, 1 to 120 characters.                                                                 |
| `text`      | Plain text, 1 to 2,000 characters.                                                             |
| `actionUrl` | Optional. `https`, on the origin of one of the application's registered redirect URIs.         |
| `channels`  | Optional, `email` and/or `sms`. Every verified channel when omitted.                           |

The response lists channels and their status, never addresses. Errors are `notice_invalid_token`
(401), `notice_not_enabled` (403), `notice_unknown_user` (404, which also covers a user with no grant
for the application, so an app cannot learn who else has an account), `notice_action_url_not_allowed`
(400), `notice_no_channel` (422) and `notice_rate_limited` (429). The limits are 300 notices an hour
per application and 10 an hour per application and user.

---

## Verify Tokens In Your API

An API that receives the provider's access tokens as `Authorization: Bearer` needs only the
issuer and its own resource identifier. The verify-only guards in every Seamless adapter check
those tokens the same way, held to shared signed test vectors, with no cookie secret, service secret
or auth routes:

- RS256 only, header `typ` `at+jwt`, a `kid` from the issuer's key set, and no `crit` header.
- `iss` equal to the issuer exactly, the audience in `aud`, `exp` required, 5 seconds of clock skew.
- `sub` and `client_id` present. A first-party Seamless session token never passes.
- A sender-constrained token (`cnf`) is refused unless you pass a confirmation hook.
- Keys come from `<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration` (its `issuer` must match, and its
  `jwks_uri` must be https when the issuer is), or from a `jwks_uri` you set. If either cannot be
  fetched the request gets `401 invalid_token`. Nothing fails open.

| Refusal                    | Status | Body `error`                       | `WWW-Authenticate`                                                    |
| -------------------------- | ------ | ---------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| No bearer token            | 401    | `missing_token`                    | `Bearer`                                                              |
| Token fails verification   | 401    | `invalid_token`                    | `Bearer error="invalid_token"`                                        |
| Missing scope (all needed) | 403    | `insufficient_scope`, plus `scope` | `Bearer error="insufficient_scope", scope="..."`                      |
| Missing role (any one)     | 403    | `insufficient_role`                | none                                                                  |
| Step-up not met            | 401    | `insufficient_user_authentication` | RFC 9470 challenge with `error_description`, `acr_values`, `max_age` |

The step-up guard takes `acr_values` (any of, and `phr` is also met by `phrh`), `amr` (all of) and
`max_age` (seconds since `auth_time`). A client credentials token verifies, and fails role and
step-up guards.

<Aside type="caution" title="Role and step-up guards need claims the access tokens do not carry yet">
  The role guard reads `roles`, and the step-up guard reads `acr`, `amr` and `auth_time`, from the
  access token. The provider's access tokens for an API carry `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `client_id`,
  `scope`, `jti`, `iat` and `exp` only, so today those two guards refuse every provider token. Use
  scope checks for provider tokens, and read the user's `acr` and roles from the ID token in the app
  that signed the user in.
</Aside>

**Express, Fastify and Next.js** (`@seamless-auth/express`, `@seamless-auth/fastify`,
`@seamless-auth/nextjs`):

```ts
import { createResourceServer } from '@seamless-auth/express'

const api = createResourceServer({
  issuer: 'https://login.example.com',
  audience: 'https://api.example.com',
})

app.get('/orders', api.requireAuth(), api.requireScope('orders:read'), listOrders)
app.post(
  '/payouts',
  api.requireAuth(),
  api.requireStepUp({ acrValues: ['phr'], maxAge: 300 }),
  createPayout,
)
```

Next.js uses `api.protect(handler, { scopes, roles, stepUp })` on a route handler.

**Go** (`github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-go`):

```go
rs, err := seamlessauth.NewVerifier(seamlessauth.VerifierOptions{
	Issuer:   "https://login.example.com",
	Audience: "https://api.example.com",
})
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}
mux.Handle("GET /orders", rs.RequireToken(rs.RequireScope("orders:read")(http.HandlerFunc(list))))
```

**Python** (`seamless_auth`, FastAPI and Django):

```python
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from seamless_auth import ResourceServer, VerifiedUser, require_scope
from seamless_auth.fastapi import RequireBearer, add_bearer_error_handler

rs = ResourceServer(issuer="https://login.example.com", audience="https://api.example.com")
app = FastAPI()
add_bearer_error_handler(app)

@app.get("/orders")
def orders(user: VerifiedUser = Depends(RequireBearer(rs, require_scope("orders:read")))):
    return {"sub": user.sub}
```

**Rust** (`seamless_auth`, axum):

```rust
let verifier = Verifier::builder("https://login.example.com")
    .audience("https://api.example.com")
    .build()?;

let app: Router = Router::new().route(
    "/orders",
    get(list_orders)
        .route_layer(verifier.require_scope(["orders:read"])?)
        .route_layer(verifier.require_auth()),
);
```

Each adapter's README lists its full verify-only API. See the [Go](/build/go-adapter),
[Python](/build/python-adapter) and [Rust](/build/rust-adapter) adapter pages for installation.

## Security Defaults

The edge's configuration is locked to OAuth 2.1 and RFC 9700. No application setting can loosen
it:

- The code flow with `S256` PKCE for every client. No implicit, hybrid or password grant.
- Exact redirect URI matching. The only exception is the port of a native app's loopback redirect.
- `iss` on every authorization response (RFC 9207).
- Refresh token rotation, with reuse ending the session.
- Audience-restricted access tokens for APIs.
- `private_key_jwt` by default, shared secrets only by opt-in, never `client_secret_jwt`.
- No dynamic client registration: applications come only from the registry.
- Errors go only to a registered redirect URI. An unregistered one gets an error page.
- Hosted pages cannot be framed, and their state-changing routes need a same-origin request.

The full matrix, with the test behind each row, is in the edge repo's
[docs/oauth-security.md](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-oidc-provider/blob/main/docs/oauth-security.md).
